comments.text: As a Singaporean, I’m not proud that we have the highest percentage of reclaimed land. Our reclaimed land uses sand harvested from riverbeds in Cambodia and Vietnam, which when extracted in excess, causes irreversible damage to the riverbed structure and affects the water’s ecosystems as well as negatively impacts people who depend on the river for a living. Our government continues to import sand from Vietnam via third party intermediaries even after we banned it on paper, exploiting legal loopholes. What do we even do with the extra reclaimed land? People are not gonna live on them or have jobs on them. We have enough space for living, we just need to cherish it. If only those capitalist property developer companies and the government weren’t so greedy, then we don’t need to reclaim more land or cut down our own forests to make “space”. We honestly really have enough and don’t need to reclaim more at the expense of the natural environments of our neighbors.

replies.text:
They do this to create artificial marshes, but it’s only temporary because the dispatched sediment eventually sinks without the natural force of water to keep it there. And it’s very expensive. 

They can control spillways to mimic the natural flooding that would have occurred without the levees. This creates land that is more resistant to erosion, but it disrupts salinity and impacts oyster and shrimp fisheries and was scrapped.

Combined with the man-made canals that cut the land up and broke the natural transition of fresh to salt water in the first place, it is an impossible problem.

Chicago has Streeterville. It isn’t very big, but it’s a great story.

Captain Streeter ran the Reaper aground in 1886 and invited dumping of garbage and debris (from the Great Chicago Fire 1871) around the ship in the shallow lake waters, creating more land around the ship.
